summary: Defines a DHCP option for authenticating DHCP messages. Newly attached hosts can be configured automatically only if they have proper authorization, and they can confirm they are talking to a genuine DHCP server.

eli5.summary: It adds a secret handshake so a new computer only takes help from the real front desk and not an impostor.

subtitle: A DHCP option that lets clients and servers prove who sent a message and that it was not tampered with.

tldr.problem: DHCP hands out addresses and settings to anyone who asks, and clients accept answers from any server, so a bogus or misconfigured server can feed them bad configuration.
tldr.mechanism: A new DHCP option, code 90, carries either a plain configuration token or a 'delayed authentication' check: an HMAC-MD5 code computed with a secret shared between client and server.
tldr.outcome: Clients can reject offers that do not validate and servers can reject unknown or forged clients. It only works within one administrative domain where a secret can be shared in advance, and DHCPDISCOVER messages stay unauthenticated.

today: RFC 3118 is a Proposed Standard from June 2001, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DHCP Needs Authentication
sections.content:
DHCP carries configuration, including an IP address, from central servers to hosts. RFC 3118 notes that some administrators want to authenticate the source and contents of DHCP messages, and to limit address allocation to authorized hosts. This matters most where the network medium is not physically secured, such as wireless networks or college residence halls.

The threat model separates the risks. A client may face a rogue server that gives it wrong configuration, either to stage a man-in-the-middle attack or to deny service, or a server that was started by accident. A server may face an invalid client posing as a valid one, for theft of service or to dodge auditing. Both sides face resource exhaustion, such as using up the pool of addresses.

The design goals, in order of importance, are to address these threats, avoid changing the current protocol, limit the state the server must keep, and limit complexity. The result combines the original Schiller-Huitema-Droms mechanism with the 'delayed authentication' idea from Bill Arbaugh.
sections.eli5: Imagine a new kid asking for a locker. Someone could pretend to be the school office and hand out a broken locker, or a stranger could pretend to be a student. This RFC gives both sides a way to check who is really talking.

sections.title: The Authentication Option
sections.content:
The authentication option uses option code 90. Its fields are Code, Length, Protocol, Algorithm, RDM, a 64-bit Replay Detection value and variable Authentication Information. Length counts the protocol, RDM, algorithm, replay detection and authentication information fields in octets.

The Protocol field names the authentication technique and the Algorithm field names the specific algorithm within it. The Replay Detection Method (RDM) says how to read the replay field. RDM 0x00 means the field holds a monotonically increasing counter, and every protocol MUST support it. A value such as an NTP-format timestamp can reduce the danger of replay attacks.

IANA creates and maintains three name spaces for this option: Protocol, Algorithm and RDM. Protocol 0 is the configuration token and Protocol 1 is delayed authentication. New values are assigned through IETF Consensus.
sections.eli5: The option is a labelled envelope. It says which kind of secret check is inside, which recipe was used, and has a counter so an old envelope cannot be sent again.

sections.title: Relay Agents and Hash Coverage
sections.content:
A DHCP relay agent may change the giaddr and hops fields of a message. So when any hash is computed over the message header, those two fields MUST be set to zero.

A relay agent may also append the relay agent information option (option 82) as the last option on messages to servers. A server that finds option 82 MUST compute any hash as if it were not there, without changing the order of options. When the server sends option 82 back to a relay agent, it MUST NOT include it in the hash.
sections.eli5: Mail carriers along the way might stamp or change a couple of boxes on the form. The secret check ignores those boxes so it does not break just because the form was passed along.

sections.title: Configuration Token and Delayed Authentication
sections.content:
With Protocol 0, the authentication information is a configuration token: an opaque value known to both sides, such as a plain-text password. The receiver compares it to the shared token and MUST discard the message if it does not match. This gives only weak entity authentication and no message authentication, so it is useful only as rudimentary protection against inadvertently started DHCP servers.

With Protocol 1, delayed authentication is used. The client asks for authentication in its DHCPDISCOVER, and the server replies in its DHCPOFFER with authentication information. Algorithm 1 uses HMAC with the MD5 hash. The sender computes the code over the entire DHCP message, header and options, and sets the secret ID field to name the shared secret that was used.

To validate a message, the receiver first checks that the replay detection value is acceptable under the RDM. It then recomputes the code with the MAC field set to zeros, and with giaddr and hops also zeroed. If the result does not match, the receiver MUST discard the message.
sections.eli5: The easy version is a password written on the note: anyone who sees it can copy it. The stronger version mixes the note with a secret into a scrambled stamp, so only someone holding the secret can make a stamp that checks out.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
In the INIT state, the client MUST include the authentication request and a client identifier option in its DHCPDISCOVER. It validates any DHCPOFFER that carries authentication information and picks from those that pass. Its DHCPREQUEST MUST be authenticated with the secret used by the chosen server, and it MUST validate the DHCPACK. A DHCPACK that fails validation sends the client back to INIT.

What a client does when no offer is authenticated is a matter of local policy. A client MUST be configurable to decline unauthenticated messages, and SHOULD decline them by default. If it accepts one, it SHOULD inform local users and log the event, because accepting unauthenticated offers leaves it open to spoofing.

The same secret is reused in INIT-REBOOT, RENEWING and REBINDING. A client MUST include authentication information in a DHCPRELEASE. For DHCPINFORM, a client with a shared secret SHOULD send the same authentication request used in a DHCPDISCOVER.

A server keeps the secrets and their identifiers, MUST save the counter from the previous authenticated message, and MUST discard any message that fails the replay check. After a DHCPDISCOVER it picks a secret, includes authentication information in the offer and records which secret it chose. A DHCPREQUEST that fails validation or names an unknown secret MUST be discarded. Whether to accept unauthenticated DHCPINFORM messages is site policy.
sections.eli5: The new computer checks every reply for the secret stamp and stamps its own requests the same way. Replies without a proper stamp get ignored, unless the computer was told it is okay to trust strangers.

sections.title: Keys and Key Management
sections.content:
Each DHCP client has a key, K. The client's key SHOULD be given to it by some out-of-band mechanism and stored locally. Each server MUST know, or be able to obtain securely, the keys of all authorized clients. If all clients share one key, they can authenticate messages from servers, but sharing is strongly discouraged because any holder can masquerade as an authorized client. To identify individual clients, each client MUST have a unique key.

Appendix A describes a way to avoid a central list of random keys. Each client's key is derived as K = MAC(MK, unique-id), where MK is a secret master key and the unique id is built from the client identifier and subnet address. The server can regenerate K on demand or precompute and cache the keys, and never needs clear-text passwords. The master key MUST NOT be stored by any client. If it is compromised, a new MK SHOULD be chosen and all clients given new keys.
sections.eli5: The office keeps one master key in a safe and uses it to cut a different key for each kid. Each kid gets only their own key, never the master.

sections.title: Limits and Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
The configuration token is vulnerable to interception. Delayed authentication does not authenticate DHCPDISCOVER messages, so a flood of them can overwhelm the server and use up its addresses. A flood of authenticated messages may also overwhelm a server as it computes keys for each one.

The RFC also lists its limits. Delayed authentication does not support interdomain authentication, so it does not address clients that roam from one administrative domain to another. It needs a shared secret for each client on each server, so it may not scale if a client connects to several domains. The text adds that a real digital signature mechanism such as RSA, while currently computationally infeasible, would provide better security.
sections.eli5: The secret handshake helps, but it cannot stop a crowd from shouting at the front desk, and it only works if the desk and the kid already agreed on a secret.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Octets in the protocol, RDM, algorithm, replay and authentication information fields.

fields.name: RDM
fields.desc: Replay detection method; 0x00 is a monotonic counter.

fields.desc: Identifier of the shared secret used to make the code.

fields.desc: Message authentication code over the whole DHCP message.

messages.note: Includes authentication information; the client validates it.

messages.note: Authenticated with the secret the chosen server used.

messages.note: Authenticated; the client must validate it.
